newsitem.title: INDIA: India eases foreign investment restriction.
newsitem.headline: India eases foreign investment restriction.

text.p: The Indian government on Friday announced the easing of a restriction on foreign investment in an effort to accelerate development of infrastructure projects.
The move would allow foreign firms, currently limited to a 49 percent direct stake in infrastructure services such as telecommunications, to take an additional indirect stake of up to 25 percent.

The government said in a statement that the Cabinet Committee on Foreign Investment took "some important decisions" at a meeting on Thursday aimed at attracting more funds into the sluggish infrastructure sector.
It exempted "investing", or shell, companies which take a stake in a joint infrastructure venture from a cap on foreign investment, even if an overseas firm owns a share of the shell firm.
Currently foreign firms can take no more than a 49 percent stake in joint ventures in the infrastructure sector, such as telecommunications, roads and power.

The cabinet committee's decision had the effect of allowing foreign firms to pump more money into Indian projects because any investment channelled through the shell companies would be considered as a domestic stake.

Under the new guidelines, foreign firms could effectively take up to a 74 percent stake in the joint venture, with 49 percent as a direct stake and 25 percent as an indirect stake through the investing company.
But the Indian partner would continue to control the joint venture.

Infrastructure companies would be allowed to bring in foreign equity through an investing company provided it was to invest in a joint venture which had won a licence to operate in a services sector subject to the 49-percent foreign equity cap, such as telecommunications.

"An investing company, by virtue of its being the registered Indian company, should be allowed to make investment in the licencee company and such investment should be treated as part of domestic equity," the statement said.
"While computing the total equity in a licencee/Indian company, only direct investment should be considered in the prescribed cap (49 percent or less)," it said.

The statement said the foreign direct investment (FDI) in an investing company "should not be set off against this cap provided the FDI in such an investing company is less than 49 percent and the management of the investing company is with the Indian owners".
The government said the arrangement would ensure Indian control over the joint venture while allowing Indian promoters to attract more overseas funds.
"The character of the holding company continues to be Indian, and all its investment in its subsidiary would be in Indian rupees," it said.
"This arrangement will also enable the domestic companies which have the inherent strength of raising finance to start up operations of their business."
